chapter_theme: The seventh ten, Kapilar's songs for Selvakkadungo Vazhiathan: the poet arrives after Pari's death, drawn by a giver who does not regret his gifts; sieges and the terms of surrender, the king defined by four exceptions, gifts to brahmins and musicians that outshine other kings as the sun the stars, two guide songs to bards, warriors fasting before a fort while palace women mark days on the wall, ancestors who ruled like him, and the ancient debts paid; the preface adds his mother's line, his sacrifice and the gift of Okanthur.

61.reading: Kapilar tells the Chera, lord of a land where the north wind carries the smell of toddy from ripe jackfruit and husband of a woman like a painted doll in a house like a painting, that since Pari of the broad chest, whose giving never dried though his sandal paste did, has gone to the far land from which no one returns, so that the drums' clay has dried and suppliants grieve, he has not come begging nor will he say less than the truth: what drew him was the king's fame, which says he does not regret what he gave nor exult each time he gives, and so he has come to the camp, rank with the flesh of strong elephants, where the singing woman's clapping hands stand in for the drum, to share a joy like a festival.
61.nuance: The poem opens the decade with Kapilar's own history: Pari is dead (line 10, வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), and the new patron is measured by a formula of giving without regret or elation (lines 12-13) that sounds like Pari's. Calling the Chera the enemy of the unnam (line 6), the omen tree, makes him a king who does not wait on signs. Line 11 is the bard's own ethic: he will neither beg nor trim his words.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's giving, which drew him after his patron's death

comparisons.tenor: the singing woman's clapping hands, which take the drum's place
the king's joyous drinking in camp

62.reading: The poet tells the victorious king, fierce as a lion, whose ornamented elephants, shields many as clouds and horses with cropped manes surround strong forts and whose fire falls on them as if suns had multiplied, that if his enemies behind moats and hill-like walls name their goads and bow and pay tribute, then their broad land will remain one fit for song, with cattle spread over grassy fields, heaps of threshed grain piled by the kaanji trees, and strong-handed toddy-drinking workers, crowned with stream lilies, waving off the striped bees.
62.nuance: The fertile farm scene of lines 13-19 is not description of the king's own land but the reward held out to an enemy who submits; the poem stops before saying what happens otherwise, and the siege of lines 1-7 has already said it.

thinai_evidence.note: the king besieges forts and offers the besieged a choice between tribute and ruin

comparisons.tenor: the bright fire that falls on the besieged fort

63.reading: The poet tells the Chera that he bows only to brahmins, his eyes are shy only before friends, his fragrant chest scarred by the bow opens only to women, and his spoken word will not fail even if the earth changes its nature; wearing the small-leaved uzhinai garland, crushing the Tamil foes with plunder and raging like thunder that shakes hills, he drove off two kings in one siege, so that the defeated warriors said they had seen his like, and since he won even with their own yoke, the poet wishes the lord of the Cheras, if any good has been done in this sea-girt world, a life of countless ages.
63.nuance: Four lines end alike (அல்லது ... அறியலையே): the poem defines the king by his four exceptions, so his pride, fear, love and truth each have one bounded outlet. The uzhinai garland of line 8 marks the deed as a siege.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's character and wishes him long life

comparisons.tenor: the king raging against the foe

64.reading: Many kings have drums of victory and true swords, says the poet, but this one, after a renowned sacrifice whose brahmins with tongues that proclaim dharma took rare vessels, has a fixed rule that when he sees musicians at the guarded gate of his sandy courtyard, where elephants wallowed in the mud of poured water, he says at once 'give them horses with cropped manes, swaying chariots and jewels'; so, as the rising sun puts out the many stars, the poet has come to praise the strong foot that broke his foes, a lord who, with the look of neythal blooming in the dark backwater, pours more benefit than the high cloud and has ended the hunger of the hungry kin.
64.nuance: The sun-and-stars simile answers lines 1-2: other kings also have drums and swords, so what makes this one the sun is the gift at the gate, not the war. The giving begins at a sacrifice, to brahmins, and passes at once to musicians.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's giving to brahmins and musicians

comparisons.tenor: the king outshining the many other kings

65.reading: The poet hails the king as chief of warriors worthy of kaanchi, whose plumed horses have hooves red from trampling corpses, wealth of those who shelter behind the bowmen's guard, husband of the red-jewelled lady whose breasts, waist, wide eyes, bamboo-like shoulders and fragrant brow are joined to a chastity that rules even the god of desire, protector of bards and treasure of gift-seekers, and says that he has happily seen the king's daily feasting assembly, where, as a master of the paalai mode on the sweet strings changes the mournful tune, the king's toddy-joy, rich in festival wealth, gives like a rain that changes things.
65.nuance: The lute simile is exact about music: the master shifts the mournful (பையுள்) mode, so the king's gift is pictured as a change of key in the suppliant's life, not merely a quantity. Line 4 recurs at 90 line 39.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's daily feast and giving

comparisons.vehicle: பாலை வல்லோன் பையுள் உறுப்பின் பண்ணுப் பெயர்த்தாங்குச்
comparisons.tenor: the king's feast turning gift-seekers' sorrow into joy

66.reading: The poet tells an old-tongued bard who goes playing the paalai mode on his great lute with its curved neck that the king, who vowed with his thundering drum and crushed the massed spears of his foes in a corpse-strewn field, gives, they say, plentiful food, elephants brought as old tribute and paddy measured in heaps, a leader like peaks clouded with morning rain who bore the enemy's onslaught, lord of a wide land where in the festival of swords warriors wear palm leaf strung with the god's tufted vaakai flower, birds, looking like those flowers, roost in the pidavu clusters by the flowering mullai of the forest, and bright gems are found in the red gravel mixed with crystal.
66.nuance: The poem is a guide song in all but its colophon: it addresses the bard and promises food. Its landscape image folds war into land: the vaakai flower worn for victory is the vehicle for ordinary birds in a mullai thicket, so the king's country itself wears his victory flower.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet directs a bard to the king's giving

comparisons.tenor: the king who bore the enemy's charge
the gleaming spears raised above the shields
the birds roosting round the mullai and pidavu

67.reading: The poet tells a skilled bard of the old city of Panthar, with his famed kin of Kodumanam, that he will receive sea pearls and fine jewels if he goes singing to the wealthy lord of high stony Neri, where the bee, sucking the open kaanthal without pause, loses its hum in dread of the hill's spirit; that lord of warriors who wear konrai garlands with white palm strips and bodies scarred by swords, hacked like the butchers' chopping block on which they cut great curved-horned bulls, has made the land tremble in many battles, with banners waving, horns and conches roaring, elephant herds moving, vultures drinking blood on fields spread with fat, headless trunks standing like sacrificial posts and the formless demon woman stirring dread.
67.nuance: The promised gifts name their sources: Kodumanam and Panthar were known for beads and pearls, so the bard's home towns are themselves the treasure. The bee on Neri that cannot hum for dread is a quiet echo of the battlefield's terror, set in the king's own hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet guides a bard to the king

comparisons.tenor: the headless trunks standing on the field

68.reading: In the camp pitched in a foreign land, where the drum beaten with fierce sticks roars through the sky like the sea with the wind for its drumstick, the king's men, who will not eat until they have stormed the fort, pass many days eager at heart and weary in body, and wonder whether, once they have taken the enemy's dwelling, they will carry off the white tusks of his riding elephants, pay with them in the market of fluttering toddy flags, and, more content than the nameless untroubled dwellers of the northern land, have many sweet delights each day; meanwhile, in the long-walled palace, sleepless women whose green jewels slip draw the passing days on the painted walls until their red fingers redden, women bound by the king's fragrant chest.
68.nuance: The poem holds two waits side by side: the warriors fasting until the fort falls and the women marking days on the wall. The akam figure of the woman counting days (compare Kural 1261) is set inside a war poem, where it measures the length of the siege. Who the wall-marking women are, the king's or the warriors', is not said; line 19 binds them to the king's chest.

thinai_evidence.note: the warriors have vowed not to eat until the fort falls

comparisons.tenor: the war drum thundering in the camp
the warriors' hoped-for life of delight

69.reading: The poet tells the victorious king, whose sky-touching banners on mountain-like elephants wave like waterfalls on peaks, whose drum roars like the wind-struck sea before an army like the sea, and who with broken swords, chosen spears, tested horses and eager warriors heaped corpses and made his enemies' families wander ruined, that those who rolled the bright wheel of rule before him surely ruled this earth because, like him, they were of unwavering purpose, and in their time the land poured its yield, the sun's heat softened, Venus stood in its good place, the sky widened and the rains answered the people's need, and the four quarters prospered together.
69.nuance: The comparison runs backwards: the ancestors are said to be like the present king (நின்போல், line 11), so he is the standard and they the copies. The good signs of lines 13-17 (the earth's yield, the gentle sun, Venus in place, timely rain) are the marks of rule that the second decade gives to the present king's land.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's army marches on and ruins the enemy

comparisons.tenor: the banners waving on the elephants

70.reading: The poet hails the king whose feet drove elephants, whose arrows harmed horses, whose spear crowded the battle and whose shoulders and strong hand bent the bow, who wears the palmyra's white leaf that bees do not hum over and flowers of sweet springs, defeated kings and destroyed their pride, husband of a lady of chastity who is true even in jest and never hears slander, and says that with his unfailing kin around him he fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, bent in gentleness but never in manhood, cared for elders more than for his young sons and paid the ancient debts, and wishes his days to be unending like high Ayirai, whose falls drop with a drum's voice heard even by the dwellers of heaven.
70.nuance: Lines 17-22 list what the king owes and has paid: gods by sacrifice (வேள்வியின்), sages by learning (கேள்வி), and elders before sons; தொல்கடன் names it as an inherited debt, not a virtue. Line 20 (வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை) puts the decade's balance in one line.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's conquests and duties and wishes him long life

patikam:7.reading: The decade's preface says that Selvakkadungo Vazhiathan, son of Porayan's queen, who was the daughter of Anthuvan of unflagging heart and long, subtle learning who bound his foes, settled lands, drove off enemies, won many battles with a dreaded army, performed a praised and ample sacrifice, went the way of dharma, held Mayavannan in his heart, gave Okanthur with its paddy and outdid the priests, and shone spotless with a generous mind; and that Kapilar sang this ten.
patikam:7.nuance: The preface names a gift the songs do not: a village, Okanthur, given after the sacrifice. Its devotion to Mayavannan sits beside the brahmin-facing duties of 63, 64 and 70.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's lineage, wars, sacrifice and gifts

links.note: Purananuru 236 is Kapilar's lament that Pari told him to stay behind and did not take him in death; Patitruppattu 61 has Kapilar, Pari gone to the land from which none returns (வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), arrive at the Chera's camp drawn by a fame for giving without regret.
links.teaches: Together they show the bard's two answers to his patron's death, the vow to be with Pari in the next birth and the journey to a new patron whose giving is praised in Pari's terms, so the Chera's praise is partly an elegy carried over.

links.note: Patitruppattu 13 sets enemy farmland ruined by the king beside his own flowering land; Patitruppattu 62 describes a rich farm of cattle, grain heaps and toddy-drinking workers as what the enemy keeps if he bows and pays tribute.
links.teaches: The second decade shows ruin and plenty as two places; Kapilar makes them two futures of the same enemy land, so the farm scene becomes the terms of surrender rather than a picture of the king's own country.

links.note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya his word will not move even if the earth moves (நிலம் பெயரினும், நின்சொற் பெயரல்) and is husband of a lady of faultless chastity; Patitruppattu 63 tells the Chera that even when the earth changes its nature his spoken word does not fail.
links.teaches: The same hyperbole for a Pandya and a Chera shows that the unmoving royal word was shared praise across dynasties, and the Purananuru poet turns it into a lever (so read the suppliant's need) where Kapilar leaves it as one of four bounded traits.

links.note: In Purananuru 107 Kapilar says Pari is not the only one who sustains the world: there is also the rain; in Patitruppattu 64 the same poet tells the Chera that he pours greater benefit than the high cloud (மழையினும் பெரும்பயம் பொழிதி).
links.teaches: Kapilar's measure of a giver is the rain in both poems, but where Pari was granted only the rain as his equal the living Chera is set above it, which shows how the poet's praise scale shifted with the patron and how far the dead friend's standard was raised to honour the new one.

links.note: In Purananuru 105 Kapilar sends a singing woman to Pari, promising jewels for his gentleness, which is sweeter than the water falling on his hill; in Patitruppattu 67 he sends a bard to the Chera, promising pearls, and fills the road with the king's battlefield of vultures, demons and hacked bodies.
links.teaches: The same poet's two guide poems show that the guide form takes its content from the patron: a hill chief is reached through his kindness and his streams, a crowned king through the terror of his wars, though both end in the same gift of jewels.

links.note: Akananuru 61 tells the heroine not to suffer looking at the tall wall where the days are marked (நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்), and pictures Pulli's men trading white elephant tusks for toddy; Patitruppattu 68 has the king's warriors hoping to trade white tusks (வெண்கோடு) for toddy while women at home draw the days on the painted wall.
links.teaches: The tusk bartered for toddy and the days scored on a wall were a stock pair of the far campaign and the waiting house: the akam poet splits them between the land the hero crosses and the heroine's room, while Kapilar keeps both inside one king's war, so the cost of conquest is counted at home.

links.note: Patitruppattu 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape its loneliness while the king lingers in camp; Patitruppattu 68 shows women in the palace marking the days on the wall while the warriors fast before the fort.
links.teaches: Two poets of two decades both end a war poem at the women left behind, which shows the waiting house was a set part of Chera praise, and Kapilar extends it from the queen alone to the whole palace and sets the warriors' own longings beside it.

links.note: Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run to the burning quarter and rain stands where wanted; Patitruppattu 69 says that under the rulers before him the land yielded, the sun's heat softened, Venus stood in its place and the rains answered need.
links.teaches: The second decade grants the good omens to the reigning king, while Kapilar grants them to the ancestors who were like him, so the same signs serve as proof of a present reign and as the inheritance a king must live up to.

links.note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty the care of five: ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself; Patitruppattu 70 says the king, with his kin around him, fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, put elders before his sons, and so paid the ancient debts (தொல்கடன்).
links.teaches: Read together, they show two accounts of what a man owes: the Kural spreads the duty over five equal claims including guests and himself, while the Chera poem counts it as an inherited debt to gods, sages and elders paid off by sacrifice and learning, so the king's virtue is framed as settlement rather than care.

source_issues: 61-70: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
62 and 68 are marked uzhinai and 69 vanji from their content (sieges, the march); the colophons give paadaan thurais, with 69 as வஞ்சித்துறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு.
68: the colophon writes செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு without the space the other colophons have; normalised in puram_thurai.
62 line 3 and 64 line 9 share the line எஃகுபடை அறுத்த கொய்சுவல் புரவி; 62 line 1 and 64 line 10 share இழைஅணிந்(து); not flagged.
65 line 4 repeats 90 line 39 and 66 line 19 repeats 76 line 14, as flagged.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 62 lines 16 and 18, 63 lines 3 and 8, 64 line 19, 65 line 2, 67 lines 5 and 22, 69 lines 8 and 12, 70 line 23; the repaired readings fit.
61 line 16 (நிலவின்அன்ன வெள்வேல் பாடினி) joins a white spear to the singing woman; the reading is odd and may hide a corruption.
patikam:7 lines 9-10 (ஓத்திர நெல்லின் ஒகந்தூர் ஈத்துப் புரோசு மயக்கி) are obscure; line 13 (கபிலர் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
